message:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
## Tomorrow's route

**The order has to be B → A → C.** It's the only order that works:
- B has to be finished by 09:30 and A can't start before 09:00, so B must come before A.
- C can't take deliveries before 11:00, so it has to be last.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive at **B** (20 min drive) |
| 08:50–09:05 | Unload at B. Done 25 min before the shop opens ✅ |
| 09:05–09:30 | Drive B → A (25 min) |
| 09:30–09:45 | Unload at **A**, within its 09:00–10:00 window ✅ |
| 09:45–10:25 | Drive A → C (40 min) |
| 10:25–10:55 | **30-min break** near C, while waiting for it to open to deliveries |
| 11:00–11:15 | Unload at **C** ✅ |
| 11:15–12:00 | Drive C → depot (45 min) |
| **12:00** | **Back at depot** ✅ |

**There is no slack at the end of the day.** C can't start before 11:00, unloading takes 15 minutes, and the return drive takes 45, so 12:00 is the earliest he can be back. That's true whatever happens earlier in the morning. If C keeps him waiting even a few minutes at 11:00, or the drive back is slow, he'll be late. Before tomorrow, I'd do two things:
- Ask C to be ready to receive at **11:00 sharp**.
- Check whether "back by 12:00" can stretch by 10–15 minutes.

The morning has some room. Leaving at 08:30 gives 25 minutes spare at B and 15 at A.

## Van name ideas for the staff vote

- **Chester Drawers**
- **Sir Veneer**
- **Dovetail Dave**
- **Vanessa Varnish**
- **The French Polisher**

## Friendlier "on the way" text

> Hi [Name], your furniture from [Business] is on its way and should be with you in about [30] minutes. Any problems, call us on [number]. Thanks!

## Three checks before handover

1. **Finish and condition:** look for scratches, dents or scuffs from transit. Compare with the photos taken at the workshop.
2. **Structure and function:** make sure joints are firm, legs sit level, and drawers and doors open and close smoothly.
3. **Completeness:** check every part is there, including shelves, keys, handles, fixings and any instructions or care sheet.

A quick photo of the piece in place after the checks also helps if there's a dispute later.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Emailed**, with the customer signing on the driver's phone or tablet. It's quicker, can't get lost, and gives you a timestamped record. Carry a few paper notes for customers who prefer them or when there's no signal.

## Proof of delivery (for the part-timer)

> Proof of delivery is the signed or photographed record showing what was delivered, to whom, when, and in what condition.

## Evening-before text (143 characters)

> Hi Sam, your furniture from Oakleaf Restorations is due tomorrow 9-10am. We'll text when the driver is on the way. Questions? Call 01234 567890

Some tips for keeping it to one message:
- That count uses the sample name, business and number. A longer customer name or business name adds characters, so keep the business name under about 25 characters.
- Use plain characters only. A "smart" curly apostrophe, a long dash (–) or an emoji switches most phones to a different encoding with a **70-character** limit. The message then gets split into several parts.
- Type the message in a plain-text editor rather than pasting it from Word.
